region.en: Guagua, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省瓜瓜（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Pampangan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 24 'The Devil and the Guachinango', eBook #8299

summary.en: A devil wins the hand of Piriang, who 'would rather have a devil for a husband'; the priest arms her mother with a Virgin image, cintas, and a sting-ray tail, and the devil is whipped into a jar sealed with holy-water cloth and handed to a guachinango to bury. Ransomed three times with money he always loses at casino, the devil wins his freedom by promising to possess the princess — and the guachinango, terrified at the third day by the cry 'Here she comes!' and the tolling bells, is married to the princess.
summary.zh: 魔鬼娶得『寧嫁魔鬼』的琵莉安；神父授其母聖母像、聖帶與魟尾鞭，將魔鬼鞭入大甕、以聖水布封口，交由闖蕩漢埋葬。闖蕩漢三次受賄埋得更淺，又三番賭輸；魔鬼終以『入公主之身』換得自由。第三日期至，鐘聲齊鳴、高呼『她來了！』——魔鬼魂飛魄散而出，闖蕩漢娶得公主。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan tale recorded by Fansler from a Laki narrator (Guagua); archival record. Fansler traces the main outlines to Spain (Caballero's 'The Demon's Mother-in-Law'), with the Cukasaptati/Tuti-nameh family behind it; the sting-ray tail is the traditional anti-aswang charm.

passages.text: There once lived in a suburb of a town a very religious old widow who had a beautiful daughter, Piriang by name. Young men from different parts of the town came to court Piriang, and the mother always preferred the rich to the poor; whenever Piriang's friends told her that the man whom she rejected would have been a good match for her, she always answered that she would rather have a devil for a husband than such a man. One day a devil heard Piriang giving this answer to one of her friends; thus encouraged, he disguised himself as a young man of noble blood and went to Piriang's house to offer her his love, and in the richness of his dress he was unexcelled by his rivals. After a few weeks the old widow told him to come prepared to be married on the following Tuesday — but on the Sunday before the wedding-day he calmly asked Piriang to take off the cross that she had about her neck, for it made her look ugly, he said; she refused, because she had worn this cross ever since she was a child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 24 'The Devil and the Guachinango'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day the mother went to the church and told the priest that Piriang's bridegroom had ordered her to take off her cross; the priest said that that man was a devil, for no man, as a son of God, would say that a cross made the one who wore it look ugly. He gave the mother a small image of the Virgin Mary, instructing her: if when the bridegroom beheld it he turned his back on her, she was to tie him around the neck with her cintas, put him in a large jar, and bury him at least twenty-one feet under the ground. That night he came with his friend dressed like him; when the old woman held up the image of the Virgin Mary, the two men turned their backs on her. She immediately wound her cintas around the neck of her daughter's bridegroom, and Piriang came in with the dried tail of a sting-ray in her right hand and whipped him as hard as she could; then the two together forced him into a large jar, and after warning him not to come back to earth again, the old woman covered the jar with a piece of cloth wet with holy water. The other devil suddenly disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 24 'The Devil and the Guachinango'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next morning a guachinango happened to pass by the house of the old woman; she called him in, showed him the jar, and told him to bury it at least twenty-one feet deep, promising him ten pesos. At a quiet place he discovered that the whispers were coming from inside the jar: 'I am a devil, my friend. The old woman forced me to go into this jar. Be kind to me, my friend, and liberate me!' 'I shall obey the old woman in order to get my pay. I will bury you even deeper than twenty-one feet.' 'If you will bury me just three feet deep, I will give you a large sum of money' — 'I will bury you just one and a half feet deep, if you can give me much money' — 'I will give you five hundred pesos. Dig the ground near the stump of that mabolo-tree. There you will find the money in a dirty black purse.' After burying the devil, the guachinango went to the village and played casino, and as soon as he lost all his money he returned: 'I will now bury you twenty-one feet deep.' Twice more the devil bought himself shallower graves — and twice more the money was lost at gambling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 24 'The Devil and the Guachinango'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Aha! I won't let you go,' said the guachinango. 'I will bury you thirty-nine feet now.' 'I have a plan in mind which will benefit you extremely,' said the devil. 'Let me ask you if you would like to marry the daughter of the king. As soon as you set me free, I will enter the mouth of the princess and go into her brains. Then I will give her a very painful headache which no physician can cure. The king will make an announcement saying that he who can cure his daughter of her disease shall marry her. When you hear this announcement, go to the palace at once, and offer your services to the king. As soon as you reach the princess, tell me that you have come, and I will leave her immediately... Do not fail to go to the palace, for I am determined to reward you for your kindness to me.' The guachinango liberated the devil and set out for the city; there he met a group of soldiers crying that he who could cure the princess should have her to wife, and a written agreement was made: failure in three days meant death, success meant marriage. But when he approached the princess and told the devil he had come, the devil refused to leave, because he wanted to get revenge: 'He further told the guachinango that he wanted him to die, for then his soul would go to hell.' More and more hopeless, on the morning of the third day the guachinango thought of a good plan: he asked the king to order all the bells of the neighboring churches to be tolled, while every one in the palace was to cry out loud, 'Here she comes!' While all this noise was going on, the guachinango approached the princess and told the devil that the old woman was coming with her cintas; when the devil heard this he was terribly frightened, and left the princess and disappeared. The next day the guachinango was married to the princess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 24 'The Devil and the Guachinango'; not verbatim.

region.en: Manila and Cebu, Philippines (narrator's home cities)
region.zh: 菲律賓馬尼拉與宿霧（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog fairy-tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), notes to Tale 24, 'Mabait and the Duende', eBook #8299

summary.en: The duende — one of the angels dropped to earth when Lucifer fell, becoming tigbalang in the forests, mermaids in the seas, and duendes in the cities — befriends the honest slave Mabait and pays him daily isabels. The envious Masama betrays him, traps the spirit under a saint's dress in a jar, and is cheated of it twice; freed on his promise to possess the king's daughter, the duende tells Masama 'Give your head to the king' when he comes, and leaves the princess's abdomen only for Mabait, who is crowned.
summary.zh: 路西法墮落時被拋下大地的天使化為林中虎靈、海中人魚、城中都恩德。都恩德與誠實的奴隸馬巴伊特結交，日日贈伊莎貝爾幣。妒忌的馬薩馬告密，以聖袍鎮住甕中精靈，兩番騙錢不開甕；都恩德以『入公主之腹』換得自由——馬薩馬趨前索婚時，只聽得一句『把你的頭獻給國王吧』；唯有馬巴伊特一到，精靈念舊情而出，他加冕為王。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog fairy-tale collected and written down by Manuel Reyes (a native of Manila, tale from Cebu), printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 24; archival record. Duende/duwende is the Philippine little-people spirit; Fansler considered this fairy-tale possibly older in the Islands than the imported Devil-and-Guachinango Märchen.

passages.text: Menguita, a king of Cebu, had two slaves, Mabait and Masama; Mabait was honest and industrious and did nearly all the hard work in the palace, so he was admired very much by the king, while Masama, who was addicted to gambling, envied Mabait. One night, while Mabait was asleep, a duende awakened him and said, 'I have seen how you labor here patiently and honestly. I want to be your friend.' Mabait looked at the duende carefully, and saw that it resembled a very small man with long hair and a white beard, about a foot high, with a red shirt, a pair of green trousers, a golden cap, and a pair of black shoes. 'Listen! When Lucifer was an angel, a contest in creating animals arose between him and God. He and his followers were defeated and thrown into hell. Many angels in that contest belonged neither to God's side nor to Lucifer's. They were dropped on the earth. Those that fell in the forests became tigbalangs, ikis, and mananangals; those in the seas became mermaids and mermen; and those in the cities became duendes.' From that time on Mabait and the duende were good friends, and the duende gave Mabait two or three isabels every day, so that by the end of the month he had saved much money and bought a fine hat and a pair of wooden shoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the fairy-tale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 24, 'Mabait and the Duende'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Masama wondered how Mabait, who was very poor, could buy so many things, and in great envy went to the king: 'Master, Mabait, your favorite slave, has a friend. This friend is a duende, which will be injurious to us if you let it live here. It will be the means of his acquiring all of your wealth and taking your daughter for his wife.' The king, in great rage, summoned Mabait and punished him severely by beating his palms with a piece of leather, then ordered his servants to find the duende and kill it. The duende hid in a small jar, and Masama covered the mouth of the jar with a saint's dress; the duende was afraid of the dress and dared not come out. 'Open the jar, and I will give you ten isabels,' said the little man. 'Give me the money first.' After Masama received the money he went away to the cockpit without opening the jar; on his way there he lost his money. He went back to the duende: 'Friend, give me ten isabels more, and I will open the jar.' 'I know that you will cheat me. Just let me come out of the jar, and I promise that you shall have the princess here for your wife.' 'How can you make her love me?' 'I will enter the princess's abdomen. I will talk, laugh, and do everything to make her afraid. I will not leave her for anybody but you.' 'Good, good!' Masama opened the jar, and the duende flew away to the princess's tower.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the fairy-tale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 24, 'Mabait and the Duende'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Only a few weeks after that time a proclamation of the king was read in public: 'The princess, my daughter, has something in her abdomen. It speaks and laughs. No one knows what it is, and no one can force it to come out. Whoever can cure my daughter shall be my heir and son-in-law; but he who tries and fails shall lose his head.' When Masama heard this, he said to Mabait, 'Why don't you cure the princess? You are the only one who can cure her. It is the duende, your friend, who is in her abdomen, and no one can persuade it to come out but you. Go now, for fortune is waiting for you.' Mabait was at last persuaded, and before going to the king first went to a church, where he prayed Bathala that he might be successful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the fairy-tale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 24, 'Mabait and the Duende'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But Masama reached the palace first, telling the king he could cure his daughter; conducted into the princess's room, he touched her abdomen and asked who was there. 'I am the duende.' 'Why are you there?' 'Because I want to be here.' 'Go away!' 'No, I won't.' 'Don't you know me?' 'Yes, I know you. You are Masama, who cheated me once. Give your head to the king' — and the executioner cut Masama's head off. Then Mabait came, and told the king that he could cure the princess; after he was given permission to try, he said to the duende, 'Will you please come out of the princess's abdomen?' 'Yes, I will, for the sake of our friendship.' Mabait was married to the princess, was crowned king, and lived happily with his friend the duende.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the fairy-tale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 24, 'Mabait and the Duende'; not verbatim.

title.zh: 胡安·薩杜特：蛇王的戒指

region.en: San Fernando, La Union, Luzon, Philippines (story very popular there)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋聯合省聖費爾南多（故事甚為流行）

texts.period: Ilocano oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 25 'Juan Sadut', eBook #8299

summary.en: His father lays the sleeping idler Juan Sadut beside a snake-hole to be stung dead — but the snake is the king of the snakes, who gives him a gold signet that advises its wearer how to obtain anything. Advised by the ring, he blinds the king's tiger with sand and red pepper, commands the cave-serpents with the sacred ring to fetch the dragon's burning stone, and answers the king's treacherous question — 'What am I thinking about now?' — in the ring's precise words, winning the princess and finally the crown.
summary.zh: 父親把酣睡的懶漢胡安放在蛇穴旁，欲借蛇吻除之——那蛇卻是蛇王，贈他一枚金印戒指，凡有所求皆能指點。依戒指之策，他以沙混紅椒迷瞎猛虎；以神聖戒指號令洞中群蛇取來龍的火石；又以戒指的原話答中國王刁鑽的『我在想什麼』——贏得公主，終承王位。

sensitivity.note: Ilocano folktale recorded by Fansler from a Zafra narrator (San Fernando, La Union); archival record. Bride-wager group with the snake-jewel; Fansler notes the tiger is not native to the Islands, suggesting Indian or Malayan tradition for the first task.

passages.text: Many years ago there lived a certain old couple who had an only son. Juan was known throughout the village as an idler, and for this reason he was called Juan Sadut; his contempt for all work was so great that he never even helped his father or mother. One day his father took him to the fields to help harvest their crops, but instead of going to work Juan betook himself to a shady spot on the edge of the field and fell asleep. His father, very much enraged, determined then and there to dispose of him: he carried the sleeping boy to another part of the field and laid him down just beside a large snake-hole, expecting that the snake, when it came out of its hole, would sting the sleeping idler, who would thus be disposed of quietly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 25 'Juan Sadut'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Juan awoke he found a large snake coiled near him; in his fright he sprang to his feet to run away, but the snake looked up at him sympathetically and began to speak: 'Why do you fear me? Don't you know that I am the king of the snakes? I am going to give you a wonderful gift that will make you happy forever.' Having said this, it dropped a gold ring on the ground, and bade Juan pick it up and wear it on his finger; the ring was of pure gold, with initials that Juan could not understand. 'Keep that ring carefully, for it will be of great use to you. Consult it for anything you want, and it will advise you how to proceed to obtain the object of your desire.' After thanking the snake, Juan set out on his travels, never worrying about his food from day to day, for from his magic ring he could get anything he needed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 25 'Juan Sadut'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In his wanderings word reached Juan's ears that the king of that country would give his beautiful daughter to anyone who could fulfil three conditions. His slovenly appearance and awkward movements only excited laughter among the nobles — 'What chance have you of winning the prize?' — but 'Let me know the conditions, and time will show,' said Juan. 'First, you must fight with my tiger, and kill it if you can; second, you must go get and bring back to me the burning stone that the dragon in the mountains has in its possession; third, you must answer correctly a question that I shall ask you.' Many a young man had risked his life for the princess's hand, but no one had yet succeeded in winning even the first contest: the king's tiger was ferocious and strong, as agile as a mouse, and the formidable dragon's breath alone was deadly poisonous, its cave guarded by poisonous serpents; every morning the dragon would come out to play with its wonderful stone, tossing it into the air and catching it in its mouth when it fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 25 'Juan Sadut'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Juan arrived home he took up his little ring: 'Advise me as to how I may overcome the king's tiger.' 'Get a handful of sand, and mix with it an equal quantity of red pepper. Take the mixture with you into the arena, and when the tiger comes near you, fling the sand into its eyes.' The next day, as the tiger advanced rapidly toward him, Juan flung the mixture of sand and pepper into its eyes; the tiger was blinded, and Juan drew his dagger and buried it deep in the animal's heart. The ring advised him for the second task: 'Go to the cave, and, in order to gain admittance, show me to the serpents. I am sacred to them, and they will fulfil whatever commands my possessor gives them.' The hissing serpents came toward him in threatening attitudes — but at the sight of the signet ring they at once became tame and showed they were glad to obey; 'Go and get the dragon's stone,' he ordered, and soon they came back with the much-coveted treasure. When the king saw that Juan had fulfilled two of the hardest conditions he became alarmed because the new bridegroom was to be a person of very low birth, and devised the most difficult question possible: 'What am I thinking about now?' Juan appeared to hesitate a moment, but he was really consulting his ring, which said, 'The king has in mind the assurance that you will not be able to answer his question.' Looking up, Juan answered in the precise words of the ring, and thus answered it correctly. Astonished at the wonderful power of Juan, the king gave his daughter to him; and when he died, the young couple inherited the crown of the kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 25 'Juan Sadut'; not verbatim.
